planting.note: Sow fresh seed on the surface of a lean, fast-draining sagebrush-steppe or rock-garden mix in fall, letting winter cold break dormancy naturally; withhold water once foliage yellows in early summer.

directions: A tough, drought-adapted shooting star for sagebrush-steppe and dry rock-garden conditions, this species occurs from British Columbia to California and east to Alberta and Wyoming in vernally moist flats and mid-elevation meadows, wanting a distinct winter-wet, summer-dry cycle rather than season-long moisture. Its narrow, slender seed capsules give it the common name slimpod, and its deep rose-pink to orchid, strongly reflexed petals distinguish it from similar relatives. Withhold all water once foliage yellows in early summer to mimic its native dry-season dormancy.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall with 1-3 months cold-moist stratification into a pond margin, bog garden, or rivulet edge with constantly saturated, cool soil and full sun.

directions: Unlike most shooting stars that go dormant by early summer, this species blooms in summer and fall at high elevation, tracking the delayed snowmelt of subalpine bogs and streambanks in the Sierra Nevada with outlying populations in Oregon, Utah, and Arizona. Site it in full sun with constantly saturated, cool soil — a pond margin, bog garden, or rivulet edge — rather than treating it as a typical woodland-ephemeral shooting star. Its narrow basal leaves and dark, slender flower stems with reflexed pink-lavender petals and prominent dark anthers carry the classic shooting-star form, but the thick perennial root system and wet-site preference set it apart from drier relatives.

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets in spring, or sow seed with an extended natural cold-moist stratification, into a consistently wet, cold bog bed in full sun; never let the bog dry out, even in summer.

directions: The most cold-hardy and northerly shooting star in cultivation, native across most of Alaska, Yukon, the Northwest Territories, northern British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Russia's Chukotka Peninsula, this species is also unusual among its relatives for spreading by rhizome rather than staying a solitary rosette. Each rhizome shoot produces several pink-to-magenta flowers with white centers, and because it spreads underground it can colonize a consistently wet, cold bog bed rather than being planted as a single specimen. Give it full sun to match its native long arctic summer days, and never let the bog dry out — the opposite cultural need from the Mediterranean-climate shooting stars already in cultivation.
sources: Wikipedia (citing NatureServe and Flora of North America)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall with winter stratification, or plant nursery-propagated divisions, into a sharply drained site mimicking basalt-cliff habitat with ample spring moisture and a dry summer rest. Source only nursery-propagated stock — never collect from wild populations.

directions: An extremely rare Pacific Northwest coastal-range endemic found at only a handful of known wild locations across adjacent Oregon and Washington counties, this species was not discovered until 1945 and not formally described until 1979. In the garden, replicate its moist basalt-slope habitat with sharp drainage, ample spring moisture, and a dry summer rest; it tolerates sun, light shade, or half shade equally well. Bright magenta petals with white bases and often toothed foliage distinguish it from the more common Pacific Northwest shooting stars, and because of its extremely restricted wild range, plants should come only from specialty nurseries that propagate it responsibly.
sources: Center for Plant Conservation National Collection

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall with winter cold stratification into a lean, sharply drained, basalt-mimicking site with full winter-spring sun; let it go summer-dry and dormant.

directions: Endemic to the Columbia River Gorge of Washington and Oregon, this species grows on open, grassy, basalt-outcrop slopes often alongside Oregon white oak and ponderosa pine, and it is typically the first shooting star — sometimes the first wildflower of any kind — to bloom in its range each year. Give it a lean, sharply drained, basalt-mimicking site with full winter-spring sun and moisture, then let it go summer-dry and dormant as the surrounding Gorge grasslands do. Its fuzzy, glandular basal leaves and pink-and-yellow flowers carry typical shooting-star form, but the nearly black pollen, versus the yellow pollen cones of most relatives, is a clean, reliable identification feature.
